title: Close enough to answer
hook: I am near, I answer the caller (2:186), set right inside the fasting verses
carry: near, in the middle of the fast

segments.voice: Yesterday, sawm, the fast, and your line: Allah wants ease for you. Where did you look for the kind version of a rule? Today, the verse that sits right in the middle of those fasting verses. Day three hundred fifty-two.

It's late afternoon in Ramadan. The fast has been long, the coffee headache came and went hours ago, and the kitchen smells of something that can't be eaten yet. Fifteen minutes to sunset. In some homes, this is when people go quiet. Someone sits with hands open. Someone else stirs the soup and whispers. Tradition counts this hour as a time when asking is heard. Part of the reason is a verse placed exactly here. Today: close enough to answer.
screen: `FIFTEEN MINUTES TO SUNSET.` → `HANDS OPEN, A WHISPER.` → `A VERSE PLACED EXACTLY HERE.`

segments.voice: Read the passage in order. Verse one hundred eighty-five: the month of Ramadan, ease not hardship. Verse one hundred eighty-seven: the nights of the fast, eating until the white thread of dawn shows against the black. And between them, verse one hundred eighty-six, which isn't about fasting at all. In Pickthall's words: “And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.” Last year you heard how this verse skips the word say, so that God answers directly. This year, look at where it was placed, and at how it ends. Read in that spot, it speaks to the hungry person: you're not only holding back; you're close. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi names three people whose supplication is not turned away, and the first is the one fasting, until they break their fast. That's why the minutes before sunset fill with whispering. Now the ending. The verse goes on: so let them respond to Me, and believe in Me, so that they may be rightly guided. The word for God answering, ujib, and the word for people responding, yastajibu, come from the same root, j-w-b. In the verse, the answering runs both ways. God answers the caller; the caller is asked to answer back by trusting and acting. And the verse sets that two-way answer among the rules for the hungry days. Near, in the middle of the fast.
screen: `BETWEEN 185 AND 187` · `I AM NIGH. I ANSWER.` · `THE FASTING PERSON IS NOT TURNED AWAY` · `J-W-B: THE ANSWERING RUNS BOTH WAYS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: whisper one du'a. If you pray, choose one thing you need, small or large, and say it quietly in your own words, the way people do in the minutes before sunset. You can begin by praising, as the Fatiha taught. If you don't pray, say one hope softly, so that only you hear it. Then sit in the quiet after it, and notice how close the quiet feels. The bell holds the time.
Suppliant. The one who calls out in prayer — the one Pickthall's verse says God answers when it is uttered in the depths of the fast. Today's word.
Your line: near, in the middle of the fast. Today, when you're hungry, tired or holding back from something, use that moment to whisper. Day three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Many Muslims spend the last minutes before breaking the fast in personal supplication, following the hadith that the fasting person's du'a is not turned away, and the placement of 2:186 among the fasting verses.

original.note: Arabic: I answer (2:186), from the root j-w-b; the same root gives yastajibu, let them respond.

trapdoor: what you thought: a general verse about prayer.
what it means: a promise of nearness placed inside the fasting verses, for the person who is holding back.
what a scholar hears: the pairing of ujib (I answer) and falyastajibu (let them respond) from one root, j-w-b, and at-Tirmidhi's hadith on the fasting person's du'a.
